KEY MESSAGE 1...Turning colder tonight with a few lake effect rain 
and snow showers.

A sharp mid level trough will cross the eastern Great Lakes 
overnight, with a cold pool aloft in the base of the trough dropping 
850MB temps down to -7C to -9C. The cold air aloft will aid in 
yielding moderate lake induced instability, with lake induced 
equilibrium levels peaking over 10K feet. Despite the instability, 
shallow synoptic scale moisture and short northwest fetch will limit 
the lake response to transient bands of light rain/snow showers 
tonight. The best coverage will be this evening when large scale 
ascent from DPVA/height falls ahead of the trough cross the eastern 
Great Lakes, with lake effect showers diminishing overnight and then 
ending altogether Tuesday morning.

Precip type will change to mainly snow overnight with the exception 
of the immediate lakeshores. A spotty light coating of snow 
accumulation is possible across the higher terrain of the Southern 
Tier, Bristol Hills, and in portions of Central NY tonight. 

Strong high pressure will build into the Great Lakes Tuesday, with 
any remaining light lake effect snow showers ending in the morning. 
Strong subsidence and drying will then allow for increasing sunshine 
later in the day. 

Temperatures will be quite cold tonight through Tuesday night. Highs 
Tuesday will only be in the upper 30s on the lake plains and low to 
mid 30s for higher terrain. The Buffalo Airport may drop below 
freezing tonight, and will almost certainly drop below freezing 
Tuesday night. Buffalo will fall just short of the all time record 
for latest below freezing temperature on record, which is November 
26th. This was a downtown record however, with this year being the 
latest freeze on record since the station moved to the Buffalo 
Airport in the 1940s. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Typical late November temperatures will continue 
through the end of the week. A widespread, soaking rainfall will 
arrive later Thanksgiving Day, with unsettled weather then lasting 
through the rest of the week.

Strong high pressure will drift east across the eastern Great Lakes 
and New England Wednesday through early Thursday, bringing a period 
of dry weather and seasonable temperatures. Dry weather will last 
through Thanksgiving morning, then a period of unsettled weather 
will return.

Strong northern and southern stream shortwaves will phase over the 
midsection of the nation, with a deep closed low developing over the 
Tennessee Valley by Thanksgiving Day. This deep closed low will then 
move northeast, reaching New England by Saturday. A surface low will 
track northeast across the Ohio Valley to the eastern Great Lakes 
Thursday through Friday, with a secondary low also moving NNE along 
the eastern seaboard. A plume of deep Gulf and Atlantic moisture 
will be captured by this system and advected northward into our 
region, enhanced by a strong southeasterly low level jet. 

A solid area of rain will overspread the entire region from south to 
north Thanksgiving afternoon, with widespread rain lasting through 
the first half of Thursday night. Friday through Saturday, 
occasional showers will continue as the deep mid level closed low 
crosses the region. The airmass will grow cold enough for some lake 
enhancement as well by Friday and Saturday, with early indications 
pointing towards westerly flow during this time frame.

The airmass will be warm enough for almost all rain through Friday 
morning, although its not out of the question a few wet snowflakes 
or sleet pellets may mix in across higher terrain at times. Late 
Friday through Saturday, modest cold advection will drop 850MB temps 
down to -2C to -3C. Forecast soundings still suggest rain for lower 
elevations, but some wet snow may start to mix in across higher 
terrain. The marginal temperatures surface and aloft suggest there 
will be little, if any snow accumulation during this period, even 
across higher terrain.

This system will bring beneficial rain to the region, with rainfall 
amounts likely reaching 1.0" to 1.5" across much of the region late 
Thursday through Saturday. Much of the area is now in D1 moderate 
drought after the exceptionally dry conditions from September 
through today.

A trough will persist over the Great Lakes Sunday through Monday, 
with a few more rain and wet snow showers possible at times.
